about.reply: A1C is a blood test that shows your average blood sugar level over the past about 3 months, and it is used to check for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes and to see how well diabetes is being managed.
about.why: It reflects average glucose attached to red blood cells, so higher percentages mean higher average blood sugar over time. The test is different from daily finger-stick checks.

care.reply: Abdominal pain can come from many organs in the abdomen and sometimes starts elsewhere like the chest, so it is best to watch closely and not assume it is mild or serious from pain alone.
care.next_step: If the pain is mild and there are no urgent signs, call a health care provider today for advice, and seek care now if pain is sudden and sharp or lasts a week or more with other symptoms.
care.why: Pain location and severity do not always match how serious the problem is, and certain combinations of symptoms mean immediate medical help is needed.
urgent_if: Sudden and sharp abdominal pain
Pain in chest, neck or shoulder with abdominal pain
Vomiting blood or blood in stool
Abdomen stiff, hard and tender to touch

about.reply: Abdominal pain is pain in the area from below your chest to your groin. It can come from many organs in that area, not just the stomach, and sometimes pain starts elsewhere like the chest.
about.next_step: Call your health care provider if mild pain lasts a week or more or if pain comes with other symptoms.
about.why: The abdomen contains many organs, so pain can have different sources. Severity alone does not tell how serious it is.
urgent_if: sudden and sharp abdominal pain
pain in chest, neck or shoulder with abdominal pain
vomiting blood or blood in stool
abdomen stiff, hard and tender to touch

care.reply: Acute bronchitis is inflammation of the airways that causes a cough often with mucus, and can cause shortness of breath, wheezing, low fever and chest tightness. At home, rest, fluids and humidified air can help ease symptoms, and fever can be managed with acetaminophen for adults as per label. Antibiotics do not help if the cause is viral, which is most common.
care.next_step: Watch symptoms at home and get medical care within 2 to 3 days if cough or breathing is not improving, or sooner if any urgent signs appear.
care.why: Most acute bronchitis from viruses gets better within several days, though cough can last several weeks after infection. A health care provider can confirm the cause by history and listening to breathing and decide if tests or inhaled medicine are needed.
urgent_if: trouble breathing or wheezing that is getting worse
chest pain or pressure
high fever lasting more than 3 days
coughing up blood

about.reply: Acute bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchial tubes that carry air to your lungs, and it usually causes a cough that often brings up mucus, sometimes with shortness of breath, wheezing, low fever or chest tightness. It is most commonly caused by the same viruses that cause colds and flu, spread by coughing or unwashed hands, and can also be triggered by tobacco smoke, air pollution, dust, vapors and fumes; less often bacteria cause it.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly if you have trouble breathing, wheezing that is not easing, a fever that stays high, cough lasting more than 3 weeks, or you are at higher risk due to age or health conditions.
about.why: Most acute cases improve within several days, but the cough can linger for weeks after the infection is gone. Antibiotics do not help viral bronchitis, so care is usually rest, fluids, fever relief and airway support when needed.

care.reply: Alcohol use disorder is a condition where drinking causes distress and harm and can involve craving, loss of control and feeling anxious or irritable when not drinking. It ranges from mild to severe and is best assessed and managed with a doctor or addiction specialist, with support from family.
care.next_step: Talk to a doctor or addiction specialist within the next few days for assessment and support options, and involve people they trust.
care.why: Risk and severity depend on how much, how often and how quickly alcohol is used, and misuse can increase risk over time. A clinician can assess safely and discuss support without you having to diagnose.
urgent_if: confusion or drowsiness after stopping drinking
seizures or shaking that won’t stop
vomiting and unable to keep fluids down
chest pain or trouble breathing

about.reply: Alcohol Use Disorder, AUD, is a disease where drinking causes distress and harm and the body and brain start to need alcohol. It can range from mild to severe, and severe AUD is often called alcoholism or alcohol dependence.
about.next_step: See a doctor within 2 to 3 days if drinking is causing distress, harm, or you notice craving, loss of control, or anxiety/irritability when not drinking.
about.why: Risk goes up with how much, how often and how quickly you drink, and with alcohol misuse such as binge drinking. Binge drinking is 5 or more drinks within a few hours for men and about 4 or more for women, reaching a BAC of 0.08% or more.

care.reply: In general, avoiding known triggers and using the medicines you already have as prescribed can help mild symptoms, and a doctor can confirm the cause with skin or blood tests and discuss treatments like medicines or allergy shots.
care.next_step: If symptoms are mild and you know the trigger, avoid it and note what happens; book a doctor within 2 to 3 days for assessment and advice on management.
care.why: Allergies range from minor to severe and can be triggered by many different substances. The right plan depends on what triggers the reaction and how severe the symptoms are, which a doctor can assess.
urgent_if: trouble breathing or wheezing
swelling of lips, tongue or throat
widespread hives with dizziness or faintness
rapidly worsening symptoms

about.reply: Common triggers are pollen, dust mites, mold spores, pet dander, certain foods, insect stings and medicines. See a doctor if symptoms bother you, keep coming back, or you have swelling, trouble breathing or a severe reaction.
about.why: Allergies happen because the immune system gives a false alarm to things that do not bother most people. Genes and environment both play a role, and reactions can range from mild to severe like anaphylaxis.

care.reply: Alzheimer's disease is a brain disorder that causes thinking and memory skills to worsen over time and is not a normal part of aging. It usually starts slowly with trouble remembering recent events, repeating questions, getting lost in familiar places, and changes in behavior, and care needs increase as symptoms progress.
care.next_step: Arrange a medical evaluation soon for assessment and safety planning, and involve family in daily support and supervision.
care.why: AD affects memory, language and daily self-care and progresses in stages, so early support and monitoring help with safety and planning. The exact course varies by person and only a clinician who examines the person can confirm the cause and plan care.

about.reply: Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia in older people and is a brain disorder that seriously affects thinking, memory and the ability to do daily activities. It is not a normal part of aging and symptoms slowly get worse over years, starting with trouble with recent memory, language and recognition. The exact cause is not fully known, but it involves brain changes that first affect areas that control thought, memory and language.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly if you or someone you know has ongoing memory loss that interferes with daily life, getting lost in familiar places, repeating questions, not recognizing family, or trouble speaking, reading or writing.
about.why: Evidence describes AD as a progressive brain disorder with worsening memory and daily function, often mistaken for normal aging but not normal. Early medical review helps distinguish it from other causes and plan support.

care.reply: Anemia means the blood does not carry enough oxygen to the body, often because of low iron or problems making or losing red blood cells. It is diagnosed with a physical exam and blood tests, and treatment depends on the kind of anemia you have.
care.next_step: Have the person seen by a doctor soon for an exam and blood tests, and sooner if symptoms are getting worse.
care.why: Anemia has many possible causes such as blood loss, low iron, folate or B12 intake, pregnancy, and blood disorders, and only tests can show the type and cause. The doctor’s plan and the report’s own reference ranges come first.
urgent_if: trouble breathing or chest pain or pressure
fainting, confusion or not waking up
very pale skin with rapid heartbeat
severe dizziness or weakness

about.reply: Anemia means your blood does not carry enough oxygen to the body because you have too few red blood cells or not enough hemoglobin, the iron-rich protein that carries oxygen.
about.why: The most common cause is not enough iron, but anemia can also come from blood loss, low red blood cell production, or faster destruction of red cells. Symptoms and the right treatment depend on the type, so a doctor needs blood tests to confirm it.

care.reply: Wash the bite with soap and water as soon as possible and keep it clean and covered. Get medical attention today for assessment, especially if the animal is unknown, stray, wild, or cannot be observed for rabies risk.
care.next_step: Clean the wound now with soap and water and seek a doctor today for bite care and rabies and tetanus advice.
care.why: Cleaning reduces infection risk and a clinician can check the wound, decide on tetanus booster need, and assess rabies risk from the animal type and availability.
urgent_if: heavy bleeding that does not stop with pressure
wound is deep, dirty, or on face/hands
signs of infection such as increasing redness, warmth, swelling, pus or fever
bite from a wild or stray animal and rabies is a concern in your area

about.reply: An animal bite is a wound made by an animal’s teeth that can break the skin and introduce germs. It is commonly caused by pets, especially dogs and cats, and by wild animals that feel threatened, are sick, or are protecting young or territory.
about.why: Bites are rarely life-threatening on their own, but they can become infected and lead to serious medical problems, and some animals can transmit rabies. Cleaning the wound with soap and water right away helps reduce infection risk.

about.reply: Antibiotics are medicines that fight bacterial infections by killing bacteria or stopping them from growing and multiplying. They are used for certain bacterial infections like strep throat, urinary tract infections and some E. coli infections, and they do not work for viral illnesses such as colds, flu or most sore throats.
about.why: Antibiotics only help when bacteria are the cause, so a health care provider needs to decide if an antibiotic is needed. Using them when they are not needed can cause side effects without benefit.

care.reply: Anxiety is a feeling of fear, dread and uneasiness that can cause sweating, restlessness, tension and a rapid heartbeat, and it can be a normal reaction to stress. Right now you can help the person rest in a calm place, slow breathing, and avoid caffeine or stimulants while keeping them safe and supported.
care.next_step: If the anxiety is new or getting worse, book a check with a doctor within 2 to 3 days, and sooner if it interferes with work, school or relationships.
care.why: Anxiety can be temporary with stress, but anxiety disorders are when fear does not go away, lasts at least 6 months, and interferes with daily life. Only a clinician who can assess the person can tell which is happening.
urgent_if: talks about harming self or others
cannot breathe, chest pain or pressure
confused or not responding

about.reply: Anxiety is a feeling of fear, dread and uneasiness that can make you sweat, feel restless and tense, and have a rapid heartbeat. It is a normal reaction to stress, like before a test or a difficult decision, and can help you cope, but it becomes a problem when the fear is not temporary and gets worse over time.
about.next_step: Consider seeing a doctor if anxiety lasts most days for 6 months or more, feels excessive, or interferes with work, school or relationships.
about.why: Anxiety disorders are defined by anxiety that does not go away, can worsen, and interferes with daily activities. The evidence describes normal anxiety versus persistent anxiety disorders such as generalized anxiety disorder and panic disorder.

care.reply: Call 112 now. Appendicitis is a medical emergency that needs immediate in-person care and usually surgery, and it can worsen quickly if not treated.
care.next_step: Get urgent medical help now and go to the nearest hospital. Do not eat or drink until seen.
care.why: A blockage can cause increased pressure, loss of blood flow and inflammation, and the appendix can burst leading to peritonitis. The evidence states appendicitis is a medical emergency and treatment almost always involves removing the appendix.
urgent_if: Pain in abdomen getting worse, especially right lower side
Fever, nausea or vomiting with abdominal swelling
Inability to pass gas or sudden loss of appetite

about.reply: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, a small tube-like pouch attached to the first part of the large intestine in the lower right abdomen. It commonly starts when something blocks the appendix, raising pressure inside, reducing blood flow and causing inflammation. If untreated the appendix can burst and spread infection into the abdomen.
about.next_step: Seek medical care the same day for sudden worsening lower right abdominal pain, especially with loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, fever or swelling.
about.why: A blockage leads to pressure, poor blood flow and inflammation, and can progress to rupture and peritonitis. Symptoms vary and not everyone has all of them, so the report's own range and a doctor's exam come first.

care.reply: Arrhythmia means the heart beats too fast, too slow, or with an irregular pattern because the electrical signals that control the heartbeat are changed.
care.next_step: If the person has no emergency signs now, book a check with their doctor within the next 2 to 3 days for assessment and guidance, and keep a note of when it happens and any triggers.
care.why: Many factors can affect heart rhythm such as prior heart attack, smoking, congenital heart defects and stress, and a family history can increase risk for some types. Only a clinician who can examine the person and check the heart can say what is happening for them.
urgent_if: Chest pain or pressure, or pain spreading to arm, jaw or back
Fainting, near-fainting, sudden dizziness or confusion
Trouble breathing or very fast or irregular heartbeat that does not settle
New weakness on one side, drooping face or strange speech

about.reply: Arrhythmia is a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat, so the heart can beat too fast, too slow, or irregularly. It happens when the electrical signals that control the heartbeat change, and it may feel like a skipped beat or a fast flutter.
about.why: The electrical signals control when the heart beats; when they are disrupted the rate or pattern changes.

care.reply: Asthma is a long-term lung condition where airways can become inflamed and narrowed, causing wheezing, coughing and chest tightness that can flare up with triggers.
care.next_step: If the person has a prescribed reliever inhaler, follow the label and use it as prescribed, and get medical care today if symptoms are worse than usual or not easing.
care.why: Flare-ups are triggered by allergens, cold air, infections, smoke and other things, and triggers differ by person. What is usual for them and what helps now depends on their own plan.
urgent_if: Trouble breathing or cannot speak full sentences
Wheezing is loud or breathing is fast and chest is pulling in
Lips or fingernails look blue
No relief after using prescribed reliever as directed

about.reply: Asthma is a long-term lung condition where the airways become inflamed and narrow, making it hard to breathe and causing wheezing, coughing and chest tightness. It is often triggered by allergens like dust mites, mold, pets, pollen and cockroach waste, and by non-allergic triggers such as cold air, infections, tobacco smoke, pollution and exercise. See a doctor for regular care and sooner if symptoms get worse than usual, happen at night, or you need reliever medicine more often.
about.next_step: If you have wheezing, cough or chest tightness that is new or getting worse, book a check with your doctor within 2 to 3 days.
about.why: Triggers vary by person and can change over time, and an asthma flare-up means symptoms are worse than usual. A doctor can confirm asthma and help make a personal trigger and action plan.

about.reply: B vitamins are a group of 8 water-soluble vitamins, including B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B12 and folic acid, that help your body get energy from food and form red blood cells.
about.next_step: See a doctor if you have ongoing tiredness, pale skin, tongue soreness, numbness or tingling, or a poor diet that may not provide enough B vitamins.
about.why: They are found in protein foods like fish, poultry, meat, eggs and dairy, and in leafy greens, beans, peas and fortified cereals. Not getting enough of certain B vitamins, especially B12 or B6, can cause anemia.

care.reply: Back pain is very common and often improves on its own with gentle care. For now keep moving gently, use hot or cold packs, and avoid staying in bed more than 1 to 2 days.
care.next_step: If pain is severe or not improving after 3 days, or if it followed an injury, book a doctor visit within 2 to 3 days.
care.why: Acute back pain usually lasts days to weeks and most cases get better with rest, over-the-counter pain relief and simple measures. Pain that is severe, persists, or follows an injury needs medical assessment to find the cause.
urgent_if: pain after a significant injury or fall
new numbness or weakness in legs
loss of bladder or bowel control
fever with back pain

about.reply: Back pain is an ache or sharp pain in the lower, middle or upper back that many people get at some point. It often comes from muscle strain, poor posture, lifting wrong, or wear and tear, and can be dull and constant or sudden and sharp.
about.why: Back pain is very common and most acute episodes improve on their own with simple care, but pain that is severe, lasts or follows injury needs medical review.

care.reply: Bereavement is the period of grief and mourning after a death, and grief can show up as mental, physical, social or emotional reactions. Right now, give gentle support, allow time to talk or be quiet, and help with daily routines like sleep, food and rest.
care.next_step: Offer support at home today and consider grief counseling or talking to a trusted person or faith support if distress feels heavy or lasts a long time.
care.why: Grief is a normal process of reacting to loss and its length and intensity vary with closeness to the person, whether the death was expected and other factors. Support from friends, family and faith can help, and grief counseling helps some people.
urgent_if: talking about wanting to die or that everyone would be happier if they were gone
not eating or sleeping for many days with worsening physical illness
feeling unable to care for self or a child

about.reply: Bereavement is the period of grief and mourning after a death, and it can show up as mental, physical, social or emotional reactions. It is commonly caused by the death of someone close to you, and how long it lasts can depend on how close you were, whether the death was expected and other personal factors.
about.next_step: If grief is making it hard to sleep, eat, work or care for yourself, or feels overwhelming after several weeks, talk to a doctor within the next few days.
about.why: Grief is a normal reaction to loss and can include anger, guilt, anxiety, sadness, sleep and appetite changes. Support from family, friends, faith and grief counseling can help, and a doctor can help when symptoms interfere with daily life.

about.reply: Birth control, also called contraception, is the use of medicines, devices or surgery to prevent pregnancy. It does not have a cause — it is a choice people use to plan pregnancies, and some methods can also help reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
about.why: Birth control is a prevention method, not a condition that is caused by something. The evidence describes it as medicines, devices or surgery used to prevent pregnancy, with some types also helping prevent STIs.

about.reply: A blood count test, most commonly a complete blood count or CBC, measures the number and types of cells in your blood such as red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets, plus related values like hemoglobin and hematocrit.
about.why: These cells carry oxygen, fight infection and help clotting, so the counts help doctors check overall health and look for patterns linked to anemia, infection, clotting problems or immune issues. The test itself is not caused by one thing; abnormal results can have many common causes.

about.reply: Blood glucose, or blood sugar, is the main sugar in your blood and your body's primary source of energy, which comes from the food you eat and is moved into cells by insulin.
about.why: Food is broken down into glucose and released into the bloodstream, and insulin from the pancreas helps it enter cells for energy. Levels commonly rise after meals and fall between meals, and targets vary by age and health.

about.reply: Blood pressure medicines are medicines prescribed to lower high blood pressure, also called hypertension, which is when blood puts too much pressure against artery walls.
about.why: High blood pressure often has no symptoms but can raise risk of stroke, heart failure, heart attack and kidney disease. Lifestyle changes like weight, activity, less sodium, avoiding alcohol and tobacco, stress management and sleep can help, but medicines are used when lifestyle alone is not enough.

about.reply: Blood thinners are medicines that help prevent new blood clots from forming and can stop existing clots from getting bigger, but they do not break up clots you already have. They are used when the risk of clots is high, such as with certain heart or blood vessel diseases, an abnormal heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation, a heart valve replacement, risk of clots after surgery, or congenital heart defects.
about.why: Anticoagulants slow the body’s clotting process and antiplatelets prevent platelets from clumping, which is why they are prescribed for those conditions. The exact need and safety depend on your personal health history.

about.reply: Breast cancer is cancer that starts in breast tissue when cells change and grow out of control, forming a mass called a tumor that can stay in place or spread to other parts of the body.
about.next_step: If you notice a new lump, breast skin change, nipple change or persistent breast pain, book a doctor check within the next few days.
about.why: It is most common in women and can start in milk ducts or lobules. There is no single common cause; risk rises with age and family history, but many cases occur without a clear cause.

about.reply: Breastfeeding is feeding your baby directly from your breast so the baby gets breast milk, which has the right balance of nutrients for growth and helps protect against some common childhood illnesses and infections. It can also be linked to lower risk of certain cancers in mothers. Most women without health problems are advised to breastfeed for at least the first six months of life, and most women with health problems can breastfeed too.
about.why: Breast milk provides nutrients and protective factors for infants, and breastfeeding has health benefits for mothers. Rare exceptions exist for certain illnesses and some medicines, illegal drugs and alcohol can pass into milk and harm the baby.

care.reply: Shortness of breath means it is hard or uncomfortable to take in the oxygen your body needs, and it can range from mild, like with a stuffy nose or intense exercise, to a sign of a serious problem. If the person is breathing with difficulty right now, get medical help promptly and do not leave them alone.
care.next_step: If breathing is hard now, fast, noisy or getting worse, seek care today; if it is mild and they are comfortable, speak to a doctor within 2 to 3 days, sooner if it is not better by tomorrow.
care.why: Many conditions can cause breathlessness, including lung conditions such as asthma, emphysema or pneumonia, airway problems, heart disease, anxiety and allergies, so the cause needs to be checked in person.
urgent_if: Trouble breathing or struggling to breathe
Chest pain or pressure
Bluish lips or face
Confusion, drowsiness or not responding

about.reply: Breathing problems mean it feels hard or uncomfortable to take in enough air, like you are not getting enough oxygen. Common causes include lung conditions such as asthma, emphysema or pneumonia, airway issues, heart disease that cannot pump enough blood, anxiety or panic attacks, allergies, and a stuffy nose or intense exercise.
about.why: Shortness of breath can be mild from a cold or exercise, but it can also signal a serious lung or heart problem. Finding the cause matters because the right care depends on what is making breathing difficult.

care.reply: Call 112 now. For a burn at home, cool the burned skin with cool running water for about 20 minutes and protect it with a clean, dry cloth. Do not apply ice, butter, oil or home remedies, and do not break blisters.
care.next_step: Check the burn size and depth now, and get medical care today for blisters, burns larger than the palm of the hand, burns on face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, or if the person is a child, older adult or has diabetes.
care.why: Cooling reduces further tissue damage and pain, and keeping the area clean lowers infection risk. Burns can cause swelling, blistering, scarring and infection because the skin barrier is damaged, and treatment depends on depth and area covered.
urgent_if: Burn covers large area or is deep, white, charred or leathery
Burn on face, hands, feet, genitals or over a joint
Signs of shock: pale, confused, very fast breathing or weak pulse
Inhalation injury: trouble breathing, hoarse voice, coughing smoke

about.reply: A burn is damage to body tissues from heat, chemicals, electricity, sunlight or radiation. The most common causes are scalds from hot liquids and steam, building fires and flammable liquids and gases, and breathing smoke can cause an inhalation injury.
about.next_step: Get medical care today for blistering, burns larger than your palm, burns on face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, white or charred skin, or if you feel unwell, dizzy or have trouble breathing.
about.why: Burns can cause swelling, blistering, scarring and infection because the skin barrier is damaged, and deeper or larger burns can lead to shock and need fluid, wound cleaning and skin care.

care.reply: COPD is a group of lung diseases that make it hard to breathe and tends to get worse over time. It happens when airways and air sacs lose elasticity, air sac walls are damaged, airway walls become thick and inflamed, and mucus can clog the airways. Most people have a mix of emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
care.next_step: Follow the care plan their doctor gave them and keep a note of breathing changes, triggers and medicines they use, and review it with their doctor within the next few days if you are unsure.
care.why: COPD is long-term and varies from person to person, so what helps now and when to seek care depends on their own history and doctor’s plan. The evidence describes the general lung changes in COPD.
urgent_if: trouble breathing or struggling to breathe
chest pain or pressure
bluish lips or face
confusion or drowsiness

about.reply: COPD is a group of lung diseases that make it hard to breathe and tends to get worse over time. It happens when airways and air sacs lose elasticity, get inflamed, make too much mucus, or air sac walls are damaged, so less air flows in and out.
about.next_step: Talk to a doctor if you have ongoing cough, mucus, wheeze, shortness of breath with activity, or breathlessness that is getting worse.
about.why: Long-term exposure to lung irritants is the usual cause, and in the US cigarette smoke is the main cause; pipe, cigar and other tobacco smoke can also cause it. Most people have a mix of emphysema and chronic bronchitis, but severity varies.

about.reply: Calcium is a mineral your body needs in small amounts to build strong bones and teeth, help muscles move, nerves send messages, blood vessels work and hormones release.
about.why: Almost all calcium is stored in bones and teeth, and you get it mainly from dairy, leafy greens, fish with soft bones and calcium-enriched foods. Not getting enough over time can lead to weaker bones and related conditions.

about.reply: Cancer is not one disease but many diseases where cells grow in an uncontrolled way and can form a mass called a tumor; malignant tumors can invade nearby tissues and spread to other parts of the body in a process called metastasis.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly for new lumps, unexplained weight loss, persistent cough or hoarseness, bleeding or blood in stool or urine, or any symptom that is new, worsening, or not going away.
about.why: Cancer starts when normal cell growth control goes wrong, often due to changes in genes. The evidence passage explains the basic definition and that symptoms and treatment depend on type and how advanced it is.

care.reply: A cataract is a clouding of the natural lens inside the eye that makes vision blurry or dim and can change how colors look. It usually develops slowly with age and can affect one or both eyes, but it does not spread from one eye to the other.
care.next_step: Book an eye check with an ophthalmologist within the next 1 to 2 weeks for an exam and advice, and sooner if daily activities are affected.
care.why: Cataracts often progress slowly and brighter light or new glasses may help at first, but only an eye exam can confirm the cause and whether surgery or other care is needed. Without treatment, vision can worsen over time.

about.reply: A cataract is a clouding of the natural lens inside your eye that blocks light and makes vision blurry or dim. It can affect one or both eyes and usually develops slowly with age as lens proteins clump together.
about.next_step: See an eye doctor if your vision is blurry, dim, or makes daily activities like reading or driving hard, or if you need brighter light or new glasses often.
about.why: Most cataracts come with normal aging, and risk is higher with diabetes, family history, or prior eye injury or surgery. Without treatment cataracts can lead to severe or permanent vision loss.

about.reply: Cervical cancer is cancer that starts in the cells of the cervix, the lower narrow end of the uterus that opens into the vagina. It usually develops slowly from precancerous cell changes that can be found and treated early with screening. Almost all cases are caused by a long-lasting infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus, HPV, which is passed through close skin-to-skin contact, usually during sex.
about.next_step: Ask your doctor when you should start and how often to have cervical cancer screening, such as Pap test or HPV test, based on your age and health history.
about.why: HPV infection is very common and often clears on its own within a year or two, but when it persists it can cause abnormal cells that may become cancer over time. Screening can find abnormal cells early when treatment is usually easier.

care.reply: Call 112 now. Chest pain can have many causes, some serious, so it is safest to treat it as urgent until a clinician checks it. Do not wait to see if it passes on its own.
care.next_step: If the pain is new, does not go away, or is with any warning signs, call 112 now; otherwise get same-day medical care today.
care.why: Chest pain is not always a heart attack, but heart problems, lung problems, digestive issues, panic attacks and chest wall inflammation can all cause it. The cause cannot be told without an exam and tests.
urgent_if: crushing pressure in chest
pain with nausea, sweating, dizziness or shortness of breath
pain spreading to arm, jaw or back
pain that does not go away

about.reply: Chest pain is pain or discomfort in the chest area. It does not always mean a heart attack; common causes include other heart problems like angina, panic attacks, heartburn or esophagus issues, sore chest muscles, lung problems such as pneumonia or pleurisy, and inflammation of chest joints called costochondritis.
about.next_step: Get medical care promptly if the pain does not go away, feels crushing or like pressure, or comes with nausea, sweating, dizziness or shortness of breath.
about.why: Many different organs and tissues in the chest can cause pain, so the cause varies from person to person. Some causes are serious and need urgent care, which is why new or worsening chest pain should be checked.

care.reply: Chickenpox is a very contagious viral infection that usually causes an itchy blistering rash with fever, headache and tiredness and lasts about 5 to 10 days. At home keep the person comfortable, avoid scratching, keep nails short, and use cool baths or calamine lotion for itch and acetaminophen for fever as per label. Do not use aspirin for chickenpox.
care.next_step: Keep the person home and away from others until all blisters have crusted, and call a doctor today for anyone who is an adult, pregnant, a baby, has a weak immune system, or has a fever that is not easing.
care.why: The rash and fever are typical of chickenpox and usually mild in healthy children, but adults, babies, pregnant people and those with weak immunity can get sicker and may need antiviral medicine. Itching and fever can be eased with supportive care, and aspirin is avoided because of Reye syndrome risk.
urgent_if: trouble breathing
not drinking or signs of dehydration
rash in the eyes
confusion or very high fever

about.reply: Chickenpox is an infection caused by the varicella-zoster virus that spreads very easily from person to person and usually causes an itchy, fluid-filled blister rash that starts on the face, chest and back and then spreads, often with fever, headache and tiredness.
about.next_step: If you or someone you care for has a fever with a new blistering rash, talk to a doctor today for advice on care and to avoid spreading it.
about.why: The virus causes the classic itchy rash and mild illness that lasts about 5 to 10 days in healthy children, but adults, babies, pregnant people and those with weak immune systems can get sicker and may need antiviral medicine.

care.reply: At home, care is mainly rest, drinking lots of fluids and using non-aspirin pain relievers as directed on the label to ease fever and joint pain. A blood test can show chikungunya, but there is no specific medicine for it.
care.next_step: Keep the person resting with fluids and monitor symptoms today, and see a doctor within 2 to 3 days if fever or joint pain is not improving, or sooner if they are a newborn, older adult, or have high blood pressure, diabetes or heart disease.
care.why: Symptoms usually start 3-7 days after a mosquito bite and most people feel better within a week, though joint pain can last months. People at risk for more severe disease include newborns, older adults and those with chronic conditions.
urgent_if: not responding or confused
trouble breathing
signs of severe dehydration such as very little urine or dizziness on standing
persistent high fever beyond 3 days

about.reply: Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne virus illness that commonly causes fever and painful, swollen joints starting 3 to 7 days after a bite from an infected mosquito. It can also rarely spread from a pregnant parent to newborn around birth or through infected blood.
about.next_step: If you develop fever with joint pain, headache, muscle pain or rash after possible mosquito exposure, see a doctor within 1 to 2 days for assessment and testing.
about.why: The virus is spread mainly by the same mosquitoes that spread dengue and Zika, and most people feel better within a week though joint pain can last months. People at higher risk for severe disease include newborns, older adults and those with high blood pressure, diabetes or heart disease.

about.reply: Childhood vaccines are shots, liquids, pills or nasal sprays that teach your child's immune system to recognize and defend against harmful germs like viruses and bacteria, so the body can fight them off without getting seriously sick.
about.why: Vaccines use killed, weakened germs or just parts of germs to spark an immune response and memory. This gives immunity to diseases that babies cannot handle well on their own.

about.reply: Children's health means physical, mental and social well-being, and it is supported by healthy food, enough sleep and exercise, safety, and regular checkups with a health care provider.
about.next_step: Book regular checkups for development review and prevention, and see a doctor promptly for significant weight change, sleep or behavior change, fever higher than 102°F, rashes or skin infections, frequent sore throats, or breathing problems.
about.why: Checkups help track development and catch or prevent problems early. The listed signs are common reasons school-age children are seen outside routine visits.

care.reply: Cholesterol is a waxy fat-like substance your body makes and also gets from animal foods. It is needed for hormones, vitamin D and digestion, but too much in blood can build up as plaque in arteries over time. I cannot tell if someone has a problem from this alone; a doctor needs a blood test and history to check HDL, LDL and VLDL levels and decide what is needed.
care.next_step: Book a check-up with their doctor within the next 1 to 2 weeks for a lipid blood test and advice on diet, activity and any medicines.
care.why: HDL is often called good cholesterol because it carries cholesterol back to the liver, while high LDL is linked to plaque buildup. Only a test and clinical review can show what is usual for that person.

about.reply: Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance found in all your body cells. Your body makes all it needs and you also get it from animal foods like egg yolks, meat and cheese. It is needed for hormones, vitamin D and digestion, but too much in blood can form plaque in arteries.
about.next_step: Ask your doctor when to check your cholesterol, especially if you have a family history of heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes or you smoke.
about.why: High LDL, often called 'bad' cholesterol, can build up as plaque and narrow arteries over time. HDL, often called 'good' cholesterol, helps carry cholesterol back to the liver for removal. Levels are influenced by diet, body’s own production and other health factors.

about.reply: Cholesterol is a waxy, fat-like substance in all your body cells that your body needs, but too much in blood can stick to artery walls and raise risk of heart disease. Levels are measured by a fasting blood test called a lipid panel that reports total cholesterol, LDL "bad", HDL "good", non-HDL and triglycerides.
about.next_step: If you have risk factors for heart disease or a family history of high cholesterol, ask your doctor when to have a lipid panel checked.
about.why: The test shows how much total and "bad" cholesterol is in your blood, which helps assess heart risk. The report's own reference ranges and your doctor's plan come first.

care.reply: Chronic Kidney Disease means the kidneys are damaged and cannot filter blood as they should, and it usually develops slowly over years. It is managed with regular doctor care, blood and urine tests, and steps to protect the kidneys, not cured at home.
care.next_step: Book a review with their doctor within 2 to 3 days for blood and urine tests and a care plan, and follow the doctor’s advice on blood pressure, blood sugar and salt intake.
care.why: Kidney damage can be silent for a long time and is only known by tests. Treatments can slow progression but cannot cure it, so ongoing medical follow-up is needed.

about.reply: Chronic Kidney Disease means your kidneys are damaged over years and can't filter blood properly, so wastes and extra water can build up and affect blood pressure, chemicals and hormones. The most common causes are diabetes and high blood pressure, and many people have no symptoms until the disease is advanced. Blood and urine tests are the only way to know if you have kidney disease.
about.why: Kidney damage happens slowly and is often silent, so tests are needed to find it. Treatments cannot cure CKD but can slow it by controlling blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol.

care.reply: The common cold is a mild upper respiratory infection caused by viruses, often with sneezing, runny or stuffy nose, sore throat, cough and headache that can last 10-14 days. There is no cure, but rest, plenty of fluids and simple comfort measures can help you feel better while it resolves on its own.
care.next_step: Use rest and fluids at home now, and watch for worsening symptoms over the next few days.
care.why: Colds are caused by many viruses and are very contagious through air, close contact and contaminated surfaces. Symptoms usually start a few days after infection and improve on their own.

about.reply: A common cold is a mild infection of the upper respiratory tract, meaning the nose and throat. It is most commonly caused by rhinoviruses, with more than 200 viruses able to cause it, and it spreads through the air, close contact, and touching contaminated surfaces then your face.
about.next_step: See a doctor if symptoms last longer than 10-14 days, get worse after improving, or you develop a high fever, trouble breathing, or signs of a sinus or ear infection.
about.why: Colds are very common and usually resolve on their own in 10-14 days. Rest and fluids help you feel better while the body clears the virus.

care.reply: Constipation means having fewer than three bowel movements a week with hard, dry stool that can be painful to pass, and it is common and often short-lived. At home you can support regular bowel habits with more fiber from fruits, vegetables and grains, plenty of water and other liquids, regular exercise, and taking time to go when the urge comes.
care.next_step: Try these general measures for a few days and note any change; check with a provider if bowel habits change, constipation lasts more than a short time, or it is painful.
care.why: Fiber, fluids and movement help soften stool and keep the bowel moving, and most cases are brief. What is uncertain is the cause for this person, so a provider can check medicines, health conditions and whether a laxative is appropriate.

about.reply: Constipation means having fewer than three bowel movements a week, with hard, dry stool that can be painful to pass. It is common and often short-lived, and it can happen from low fiber intake, not drinking enough fluids, too little exercise, ignoring the urge to go, or some medicines.
about.why: Constipation is defined by frequency and stool consistency, and common contributors are diet, fluids, activity and medicines. Most cases are temporary, but a change in bowel habits should be checked.

care.reply: For a cough at home, keep the airways moist with water and steam, and rest, and avoid smoke and irritants. Most acute coughs from a cold or flu settle in 2 to 3 weeks, while a cough lasting longer than 2 to 3 weeks is considered chronic.
care.next_step: Watch for 2 to 3 weeks and see a doctor if the cough lasts longer than 3 weeks, is getting worse, or is interfering with sleep or daily activities.
care.why: Coughing is a reflex to clear the throat and airways and is common with colds, flu and acute bronchitis. Chronic cough can be linked to asthma, allergies, COPD, GERD, smoking, throat disorders or some medicines, so duration and associated signs matter.
urgent_if: trouble breathing or wheezing
chest pain or pressure
coughing up blood
fever not coming down or child under 3 months with fever

about.reply: Cough is a reflex that helps clear your throat and airways. It is common with colds, flu and acute bronchitis, and can also be caused by asthma, allergies, smoking, GERD, chronic bronchitis, COPD, throat disorders and some medicines.
about.why: Acute coughs usually start suddenly and last no more than 2 to 3 weeks, while coughs lasting longer than 2 to 3 weeks are considered chronic and have different causes.

care.reply: Dehydration means the body has lost more fluid than it has taken in, so it cannot work properly. At home, the usual first step is to offer fluids in small, frequent sips if the person is awake and can swallow safely, and watch for signs of worsening.
care.next_step: If they can swallow safely, offer water or an oral rehydration solution in small sips now and check for urine output and symptoms over the next few hours; seek care today if symptoms are present or they are an older adult, infant or young child.
care.why: Fluid loss from diarrhea, vomiting, sweating, fever or not drinking enough can lead to the symptoms listed in the evidence, and risk is higher in older adults, infants and people with chronic illness. What is safe to give and how much depends on age and ability to swallow, so a clinician’s plan comes first.
urgent_if: Not responding or hard to wake
Confused, very drowsy or dizzy and cannot stand
No urine for many hours or very dark urine with dry mouth
Infant under 3 months with fever or no wet diapers for 3 hours

about.reply: Dehydration is when your body loses more fluid than you take in, so it does not have enough fluid to work properly. It commonly happens with diarrhea, vomiting, heavy sweating, fever, urinating a lot from medicines or illness, and not drinking enough water. See a doctor promptly if you have signs like very little or dark urine, dizziness, dry mouth, unusual sleepiness, or if an infant has no wet diaper for 3 hours or more, cries without tears, or has a high fever.
about.next_step: If you have any of those signs, get medical care today; for an infant under 3 months with fever, seek care now.
about.why: Fluid loss from diarrhea, vomiting, sweating and fever, plus low intake, reduces the body's water balance. Older adults, infants and people with chronic illness are more prone because thirst or fluid loss can be altered.

care.reply: Dementia is a serious disorder where memory, language, problem solving, attention and everyday tasks are affected enough to interfere with daily life, and it is not a normal part of aging. It is a general term for several neurodegenerative conditions, the most common being Alzheimer’s disease, with others such as Lewy body dementia and frontotemporal disorders.
care.next_step: Book an appointment with a doctor soon for assessment and a safety plan at home, and keep a simple diary of changes you notice.
care.why: A doctor needs to check the person’s history, thinking and daily function and rule out reversible causes. The plan depends on the type of dementia and the person’s safety needs, which can only be decided after an exam.
urgent_if: sudden confusion or not recognising familiar people
new trouble walking or falls
not eating or drinking, or getting lost and unsafe at home
signs of depression or hopelessness

about.reply: Dementia is a serious loss of mental functions like memory, language, problem solving and daily tasks that is severe enough to interfere with daily life, and it is not a normal part of aging.
about.why: It is caused by brain cell loss or damage. The most common type is Alzheimer's disease, with other common types including Lewy body dementia and frontotemporal disorders.

care.reply: Dengue is a viral infection spread by the bite of an infected mosquito. It does not spread directly from person to person. At home, rest, drink plenty of fluids and avoid medicines that can irritate the stomach or increase bleeding risk until a clinician advises you.
care.next_step: Get a medical check today for fever with suspected dengue, and have a clinician review warning signs daily until the fever is gone and the person is improving.
care.why: Symptoms usually last 2 to 7 days and about 1 in 4 infected people get sick. Severe dengue can develop, especially after a previous dengue infection, in pregnancy or in infants, so monitoring is important.
urgent_if: Severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting
Bleeding from gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, or easy bruising
Extreme tiredness, restlessness or confusion
Difficulty breathing or feeling very weak

about.reply: Dengue is a viral infection spread to people by the bite of an infected mosquito, and it is common in warm wet areas and more often in rainy seasons. It does not spread directly from person to person. About one in four infected people get sick with fever, nausea and vomiting, rash, and aches especially behind the eyes, muscles, joints or bones that usually last 2 to 7 days.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly for fever with severe body aches, persistent vomiting, bleeding signs, abdominal pain, or if you have had dengue before, are pregnant or an infant.
about.why: The mosquito bite is the usual cause, and severe dengue can develop with warning signs of shock, internal bleeding and organ problems. Risk is higher after a previous dengue infection, in pregnancy and in infants.

care.reply: Depression is more than feeling sad for a few days; it is a serious mood disorder that can affect thinking, feeling and daily activities like sleeping, eating and working, and it often needs long-term support. Right now, keep the person safe, listen without judgment, encourage regular routines and gentle activity, and avoid giving medical advice or medicines.
care.next_step: Arrange a check with a doctor or mental health professional soon, ideally within the next few days, and sooner if daily functioning is falling or mood is worsening.
care.why: Early help can help manage symptoms, and depression can last weeks to years and affect basic activities. The exact cause and best plan can only be decided after an in-person assessment.
urgent_if: Talk of suicide, self-harm or 'everyone would be happier if I was gone'
Hopelessness with giving up on daily care
Not eating or drinking for a long time or unable to sleep at all
Sudden confusion, not responding or unsafe behaviour

about.reply: Depression is more than feeling sad or irritable for a few days; it is a serious mood disorder that can affect how you think, feel and do everyday activities like sleeping, eating or working.
about.next_step: Talk to a doctor if low mood or loss of interest lasts at least two weeks or makes daily life difficult.
about.why: Depression often needs long-term treatment and getting help early can help manage symptoms. The exact cause is not always known and can vary between people.

care.reply: Diabetes means blood glucose stays too high because the body makes little or no insulin or cannot use insulin well, so glucose stays in the blood instead of reaching cells. General care is about following a doctor-made plan for food, activity, medicines and regular checks, and keeping a record of readings and symptoms. Do not start, stop or change medicines on your own.
care.next_step: Have the person see their doctor soon for a personal diabetes plan and to learn how to check blood sugar safely.
care.why: High blood glucose over time can lead to serious health problems, but steps to manage diabetes can help reduce that risk. What is safe and needed depends on the type of diabetes and the person's history, which only their doctor knows.
urgent_if: confused, drowsy or not responding
trouble breathing
chest pain or pressure
not waking up

about.reply: Diabetes is when blood sugar stays too high because the body makes little or no insulin, or the cells do not respond well to insulin, so glucose stays in the blood instead of entering cells for energy.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly if you have frequent urination, increased thirst, unexplained weight loss, blurred vision, or cuts that heal slowly, and seek care sooner if you have very high blood sugar symptoms like nausea, vomiting, rapid breathing or confusion.
about.why: Insulin made by the pancreas moves glucose from blood into cells. When insulin is missing or not working well, glucose builds up in blood and can lead to health problems over time. Type 1 is immune attack on insulin cells, type 2 is common and linked to insulin resistance, and gestational diabetes can occur in pregnancy.

care.reply: Type 1 diabetes means the body makes little or no insulin, so blood glucose stays too high and needs medical care and monitoring. It is not something you can manage at home without a doctor’s plan, and the person needs regular medical follow-up for safety.
care.next_step: Arrange a medical evaluation soon, ideally today, to get a proper diagnosis and a care plan from a doctor.
care.why: Without insulin glucose cannot enter cells for energy, and high blood glucose over time can harm heart, eyes, kidneys, nerves and teeth. DKA can develop when insulin is very low and is life-threatening.
urgent_if: vomiting and stomach pain
rapid or deep breathing
fruity-smelling breath
confusion, drowsiness or not waking up

about.reply: Type 1 diabetes means your body makes little or no insulin, so glucose stays high in the blood instead of moving into cells for energy. It is an autoimmune condition where the immune system mistakenly attacks the insulin-making cells in the pancreas.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly if you have increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or nausea/vomiting, and seek urgent care right away for vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing, fruity-smelling breath or confusion which can signal diabetic ketoacidosis.
about.why: Without insulin, glucose cannot enter cells and the liver breaks down fat, producing ketones that can build up to dangerous levels. Genes and environmental factors may trigger the autoimmune attack, and it often starts in children and young adults but can appear at any age.

care.reply: Type 2 diabetes means blood glucose stays too high because the body does not use insulin well, so glucose builds up in the blood instead of entering cells for energy. It often develops with insulin resistance that can be influenced by weight, activity level, genetics and family history, and it usually needs long-term management rather than a one-time fix.
care.next_step: Book a check with their doctor soon to get a personal care plan for blood sugar monitoring, food, activity and medicines, and keep follow-up appointments as advised.
care.why: Over time high blood glucose can cause health problems, but steps to manage diabetes can help reduce those risks. The exact plan depends on the person’s history, tests and doctor’s advice.
urgent_if: confused, drowsy or not responding
trouble breathing
chest pain or pressure
not waking up

about.reply: Type 2 diabetes is when blood sugar stays too high because your body doesn't make enough insulin or doesn't use it well, so glucose builds up in the blood instead of entering cells for energy.
about.next_step: Talk to a doctor if you have increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, fatigue or blurred vision, or if you have risk factors like being over 45, overweight or a family history.
about.why: Insulin normally moves glucose from blood into cells. In type 2 diabetes insulin resistance develops first, then the body can't make enough insulin, so blood glucose rises over time.

about.reply: A diabetic diet is a way of choosing foods, especially carbohydrates, to help keep blood glucose in a healthy range for you. It focuses on balanced meals with carbs, protein and fibre, and limiting sugary drinks, sweets and refined carbs that raise blood sugar quickly.
about.next_step: If you have symptoms like increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, or a family history of diabetes, book a check with your doctor within the next few days for blood sugar testing and personalised advice.
about.why: Glucose from carbohydrate foods enters the blood and insulin helps move it into cells for energy. With type 1 diabetes the body makes little or no insulin, and with type 2 it does not make or use insulin well, so glucose builds up in the blood.

care.reply: For acute diarrhea at home, the usual first steps are rest, frequent small sips of clean water or oral rehydration solution, and careful hand and food hygiene to avoid spread.
care.next_step: Keep fluids going and watch for warning signs today, and seek a doctor within 2 to 3 days if diarrhea lasts more than a few days, is getting worse, or if the person is a baby under 3 months, very weak, or cannot keep fluids down.
care.why: Acute diarrhea is common and often short-lived, but diarrhea lasting more than a few days may signal a more serious problem and chronic diarrhea is defined as lasting at least four weeks. Common causes in general include contaminated food or water, viruses, parasites, medicines, food intolerances and diseases affecting the gut, but the cause for this person
urgent_if: blood in stool
signs of dehydration such as very little urine, dry mouth, dizziness or sunken eyes
fever that is high or not coming down
severe abdominal pain

about.reply: Diarrhea is loose, watery stools three or more times in one day.
about.why: The most common causes are infections from contaminated food or water, viruses like norovirus and rotavirus, parasites, some medicines, food intolerances such as lactose, and diseases that affect the stomach, small intestine or colon.

care.reply: Dizziness is feeling lightheaded or unsteady, while vertigo is the feeling that you or the room is spinning, and both can be worsened by standing up or moving the head.
care.next_step: Keep the person sitting or lying down in a safe place, avoid sudden position changes, and have them seen by a doctor within 2 to 3 days for new or repeated dizziness or vertigo.
care.why: Common contributors include a sudden drop in blood pressure, dehydration, getting up too quickly, certain medicines, inner ear problems like BPPV, motion sickness, migraines and head injury. The cause is uncertain without an exam.
urgent_if: Cannot be woken or not responding
Sudden worst headache or confusion
Chest pain or pressure
Trouble breathing

about.reply: Dizziness is feeling lightheaded, woozy or unsteady on your feet, while vertigo is the feeling that you or the room is spinning even when nothing is moving. Both can get worse with walking, standing up or moving your head and may come with nausea, vomiting, sweating, trouble walking or ringing in the ears.
about.next_step: Talk to a doctor if dizziness or vertigo is new, lasts more than a day or two, interferes with walking or daily tasks, or follows a head injury.
about.why: They are different sensations but often mixed up. Common causes include sudden drop in blood pressure, dehydration, getting up too quickly, certain medicines, inner ear problems like BPPV or Meniere's disease, motion sickness, migraines and head injury. The cause is found by history, exam of hearing, balance and walking, sometimes imaging.

care.reply: Drug reactions include side effects, drug interactions and drug allergies. Side effects are unwanted effects from a medicine, interactions happen when a medicine acts differently with another drug, food, supplement or medical condition, and allergies can range from mild skin reactions to life-threatening responses.
care.next_step: If someone at home is taking a medicine and develops new or worsening symptoms, note the medicine name, dose time and symptoms and contact their doctor today for advice. Do not stop a prescribed medicine without medical guidance.
care.why: Reactions can be mild and settle, but interactions and allergies can make a drug more or less effective or cause serious harm. The report's own range and the doctor's plan come first, and only a clinician who knows the person can decide if a medicine should be changed.
urgent_if: trouble breathing or wheezing
swelling of lips, tongue or throat
widespread hives with dizziness
severe skin blistering or peeling

about.reply: Drug reactions are unwanted effects from medicines, including side effects, allergies and interactions with other drugs, foods, supplements or medical conditions.
about.why: Medicines can be helpful but may cause mild effects like stomach ache or drowsiness, or more serious reactions when they interact with another drug or a health condition. The exact risk depends on the medicine and the person.

care.reply: Dry mouth, also called xerostomia, means you don’t have enough saliva to keep the mouth wet. It can make chewing, swallowing and talking uncomfortable and raises risk for tooth decay and mouth infections.
care.next_step: Try simple comfort measures now like sipping water often, chewing sugar-free gum, and avoiding dry, salty or very hot foods and tobacco; see a doctor within 2 to 3 days if dryness is all or most of the time.
care.why: Saliva moistens food, washes away food pieces and contains minerals and antibodies that help protect teeth and the mouth. Dryness that is occasional with stress is common, but persistent dryness can be from medicines, conditions like Sjögren’s disease, HIV, salivary gland disorders, diabetes or radiation therapy.

about.reply: Dry mouth, also called xerostomia, means you don’t have enough saliva to keep your mouth wet. It can make chewing, swallowing and talking difficult and raises risk for tooth decay and mouth infections.
about.next_step: See a doctor if dry mouth happens all or most of the time, or if it makes eating, swallowing or speaking hard, or you get frequent mouth sores or tooth decay.
about.why: Saliva moistens food, washes away food pieces, supplies minerals and antibodies that protect teeth and mouth. Causes are common and varied, so a clinician needs to check medicines and health conditions.

care.reply: Ear infections often improve on their own, but a health care provider needs to look inside the ear with an otoscope to confirm it and decide care. At home, comfort measures and pain relief as advised by a provider can help while you wait to be seen.
care.next_step: Have a health care provider check the ear today if there is ear pain, fever, fluid draining from the ear, trouble sleeping, balance difficulty or hearing change, and sooner for a baby under 3 months with fever.
care.why: The middle ear can fill with fluid and mucus which affects hearing and causes pain. Diagnosis needs an in-person exam, and young babies and severe or recurrent infections are more likely to need prompt treatment.
urgent_if: baby under 3 months with fever
high fever with severe ear pain
fluid draining from ear with worsening redness or swelling
trouble breathing or not responding

about.reply: An ear infection, often otitis media, is an infection of the middle ear where the small tubes inside the ear become clogged with fluid and mucus, which can affect hearing because sound cannot get through. It is most common in young children, with three out of four having at least one by age three, and adults can get it too but less often. Signs can include ear tugging, more crying, fluid draining from the ear, trouble sleeping, balance difficulties and hearing problems.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly if your child has ear pain, fever, fluid draining from the ear, trouble sleeping, or signs of hearing or balance change, and seek care sooner for babies under 3 months with fever.
about.why: The middle ear needs clear tubes for sound to pass; fluid and mucus buildup from infection blocks that passage. Infections often improve on their own, but young babies and severe cases need medical assessment.

care.reply: Epilepsy is a brain disorder that causes recurring seizures when nerve cells send out wrong signals, and medicines can control seizures for most people once a doctor confirms the diagnosis. During a seizure, keep the person safe from injury, do not restrain them or put anything in their mouth, and time how long it lasts.
care.next_step: Get medical care today for evaluation and a treatment plan, and ask the doctor how to manage seizures at home and when to seek urgent care.
care.why: Doctors use brain scans and other tests to diagnose epilepsy and start treatment right away, because there is no cure but seizures can often be controlled. The exact cause is often unknown and management depends on the person’s history and tests.
urgent_if: Seizure lasts more than 5 minutes
Person is injured, has trouble breathing or turns blue
Repeated seizures without recovery in between
First ever seizure or new seizure in a child

about.reply: Epilepsy is a brain disorder that causes recurring seizures when clusters of nerve cells send out the wrong signals, which can cause strange sensations, muscle spasms or loss of consciousness.
about.why: Seizures happen because of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Causes can include illness, brain injury and abnormal brain development, but in many cases the cause is unknown.

about.reply: Exercise is any movement that gets your body moving, and physical fitness is your body’s ability to do daily activities with energy and strength. Regular exercise improves overall health and lowers risk for many long-term diseases, and fitness is built by making activity a habit and building up slowly.
about.why: Exercise includes aerobic, strength, flexibility and balance activities. It is not a condition that is caused by something, so there is no common cause to treat.

care.reply: Eye infections can cause redness, itching, swelling, discharge, pain or vision changes and can affect one or both eyes. At home keep hands clean, avoid touching or rubbing the eyes, do not share towels or pillowcases, and avoid contact lenses until checked. Do not start eye drops or creams on your own.
care.next_step: Get a doctor's check today for any eye infection, and sooner if there is pain, vision change, or swelling that is getting worse.
care.why: Treatment depends on the cause and the part of the eye involved, and some infections are very contagious. A clinician needs to see the eye to decide if compresses, drops, creams or antibiotics are needed.
urgent_if: sudden loss of vision or blurred vision
severe eye pain or light sensitivity
swelling spreading to face or fever
eye injury or chemical splash

about.reply: An eye infection is when bacteria, fungi or viruses infect a part of the eye and can affect one or both eyes. Common causes are infection leading to conjunctivitis, also called pink eye, and a stye, which is a bacterial bump on the eyelid from skin bacteria entering an eyelash follicle.
about.next_step: See a doctor within 1 to 2 days if you have redness, itching, swelling, discharge, pain or any change in vision, or if symptoms are not improving with simple care.
about.why: Symptoms like redness, itching, swelling, discharge, pain or vision problems can occur with eye infections, and treatment depends on the cause and may include compresses, eye drops, creams or antibiotics.

care.reply: If someone has just fallen, check them now for injury and do not move them if they have pain, especially in hip, wrist or head. Keep the area safe, help them sit or lie comfortably and watch for any warning signs.
care.next_step: If they fell just now, check for injury and get medical care today if there is pain, swelling, bruising, inability to move a limb, head hit, dizziness or confusion. For repeated falls, book a doctor visit within 2 to 3 days for a fall risk check.
care.why: Falls can cause fractures and serious injury, especially in older adults, and repeated falls often relate to balance, vision, medicines, muscle weakness or illnesses like low blood pressure or diabetes. The evidence shows risk is higher with those factors and can lead to disability.
urgent_if: Not responding or unconscious
Heavy bleeding
Suspected head injury with confusion, vomiting or loss of consciousness
Hip or leg pain with inability to bear weight

about.reply: A fall is when you lose your balance and land on the floor or ground, and it can happen at any age. It is more serious in older adults because they are more likely to break a bone, especially the hip, which can lead to disability and loss of independence.
about.why: Falls happen when balance, strength or footing is lost. Common contributors are balance problems, some medicines, vision problems, alcohol, muscle weakness in the legs, low blood pressure, diabetes, neuropathy, slow reflexes, and tripping or slipping.

care.reply: Fatigue is a feeling of weariness, tiredness or lack of energy that can interfere with daily activities. It is common with poor sleep, stress, alcohol or caffeine use, and can also be a sign of an underlying physical or mental condition.
care.next_step: Note how long it has lasted, sleep and stress patterns, and any other symptoms, and book a check with a doctor if tiredness has lasted for weeks or is affecting daily life.
care.why: Fatigue is a symptom, not a disease, and can be caused by many things including medical problems, treatments, sleep disorders and lifestyle habits. The cause is uncertain without an exam and history.

about.reply: Fatigue is a feeling of weariness, tiredness or lack of energy that can interfere with daily activities. It can be normal after activity, stress, boredom or poor sleep, but it can also be a symptom of a physical or mental condition.
about.next_step: Contact your health care provider if you have been feeling tired for weeks.
about.why: Fatigue is not a disease itself; it has many possible causes including medical problems, treatments and lifestyle habits. A provider can help find the cause and suggest ways to relieve it.

care.reply: Fever means body temperature is higher than normal and is often the body’s way of fighting an infection. For now keep the person comfortable, offer regular sips of water or oral fluids, rest, and dress lightly. Do not give aspirin to children.
care.next_step: Check temperature with a thermometer and note how high it is and how long it lasts. If fever is in an adult without red-flag signs, you can watch for 24 to 48 hours with fluids and rest, and seek care sooner if it is not coming down or you are worried.
care.why: Most fevers are from infections and often improve with supportive care, but the cause and safe treatment depend on age, how high the fever is, and other symptoms. The report’s own range and a clinician’s plan come first.
urgent_if: Baby under 3 months with fever
Trouble breathing or chest pain
Confusion, drowsiness or not waking up
Fever with stiff neck, rash that does not fade on pressure, or vomiting blood

about.reply: Fever is a body temperature higher than normal, usually around 98.6°F or 37°C, and it is a sign your body is trying to fight an illness or infection. Most fevers are caused by infections, but medicines, heat illness, autoimmune conditions, cancers and some vaccines can also cause fever.
about.why: Fever itself is not a disease but a response that makes it harder for bacteria and viruses to survive and activates the immune system. The cause and how high the fever is determine whether medical care is needed.

care.reply: Flu is a viral respiratory infection that often starts suddenly with fever, cough, sore throat, body aches and tiredness. At home focus on rest, fluids and fever comfort measures, and keep the person away from others to reduce spread.
care.next_step: Watch for worsening symptoms and seek care today if fever is high, breathing is hard, or symptoms are not improving after 3-4 days.
care.why: Flu spreads by droplets from coughing, sneezing or talking and by touching contaminated surfaces. Symptoms usually come on suddenly and can be mild or serious, especially in older adults, babies and people with chronic illness.
urgent_if: trouble breathing or chest pain
confusion or not waking up normally
fever in a baby under 3 months
signs of dehydration such as no urine for many hours

about.reply: Flu, also called influenza, is a respiratory infection caused by flu viruses that spread mainly through coughs, sneezes and talking, and less often by touching contaminated surfaces then your mouth, nose or eyes. Symptoms usually start suddenly with fever or chills, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle aches, headache and tiredness, sometimes with vomiting and diarrhea in children.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly if you have fever with flu symptoms and you are over 65, a newborn, pregnant, or have a chronic illness, or if symptoms are severe or not improving.
about.why: The flu can be mild but can become serious or deadly for older adults, babies and people with chronic illnesses. The sudden onset and fever help distinguish it from a cold, which usually starts slowly.

care.reply: If someone may have had a food allergy reaction, stop any suspected food now and watch them closely for breathing or swelling changes. Do not give more food or medicine unless a doctor has already prescribed it for them.
care.next_step: If there are no breathing, throat or widespread symptoms, keep them calm and seated, and call their doctor today for advice on what to avoid and how to plan for future reactions.
care.why: Food allergy is an abnormal immune reaction to certain foods that can range from mild to serious or life-threatening. The plan changes quickly if breathing, swelling or circulation signs appear.
urgent_if: Trouble breathing or wheezing
Swelling of lips, tongue or throat
Widespread hives with dizziness or faintness
Repeated vomiting or sudden sleepiness

about.reply: A food allergy is when your immune system mistakenly treats certain foods as harmful and reacts to them, which can range from mild to serious or life-threatening. It is different from a food intolerance, which usually only causes digestive symptoms like bloating and gas and is not an immune reaction.
about.why: The immune reaction can cause symptoms beyond digestion and may worsen quickly. Common triggers are cow's milk, eggs, crustacean shellfish, fish, peanuts, sesame, soy, tree nuts and wheat.

care.reply: For foodborne illness at home, the usual first steps are rest and replacing lost fluids and electrolytes to prevent dehydration, and keeping food safe to avoid spreading it further.
care.next_step: Watch hydration and symptoms closely today, and get medical care within 24 hours if vomiting or diarrhea is frequent, or sooner if any urgent signs appear.
care.why: Most foodborne illnesses are acute and often improve on their own, but dehydration can become serious quickly. A health care provider can confirm the cause and decide if medicines or hospital treatment are needed.
urgent_if: Not able to keep fluids down
Signs of dehydration such as very little urine, dry mouth, dizziness
Fever that is high or not coming down
Blood in vomit or stool

about.reply: Foodborne illness is sickness from eating food contaminated with bacteria, viruses, parasites or harmful chemicals. It often causes upset stomach, abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fever and dehydration, and usually comes on suddenly and lasts a short time.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly if symptoms are severe, last more than a couple of days, you have high fever, signs of dehydration, or you are pregnant, elderly or have a weak immune system.
about.why: Contamination can happen at farms, processing, transport or in your kitchen, for example leaving food out more than 2 hours at room temperature. Most people recover on their own with fluids, but some need medical treatment.

care.reply: A fracture is a break in a bone and it needs prompt medical care. Do not move the injured part and keep the person still and comfortable until help arrives.
care.next_step: Get medical care now, today. If you think a bone is broken, do not try to straighten it and seek a doctor or hospital right away.
care.why: Fractures are usually caused by injuries and can be serious. Symptoms often include intense pain, deformity, swelling and bruising, and care is needed to check the type of break and prevent further harm.
urgent_if: Intense pain with a limb that looks out of place
Open wound with bone visible
Numbness, tingling or loss of movement
Heavy swelling or bleeding

about.reply: A fracture is a break in a bone. It is commonly caused by injuries like car accidents, falls or sports injuries, and by overuse or repetitive motions; low bone density and osteoporosis also make bones more likely to break.
about.why: Fractures can be partial or complete and may be closed or open if the bone breaks through the skin. Symptoms often include intense pain, swelling, bruising and deformity, so medical care is important if you think you have one.

care.reply: Fungal infections often start on the skin or in the lungs from spores in air, soil or on the body, and they are more likely when the immune system is weak or after antibiotics.
care.next_step: Keep the affected area clean and dry, avoid sharing towels or clothes, and have a doctor look at it within 2 to 3 days if it is not clearly improving or if you are unsure what it is.
care.why: Skin and nail fungal infections can sometimes be treated with medicine applied directly to the area, while serious infections may need oral antifungal medicine. The report's own range and a doctor's exam decide what is needed for this person.
urgent_if: spreading redness with fever
trouble breathing or chest pain
skin infection with pus and rapid worsening
person has weakened immune system and infection is getting worse

about.reply: A fungal infection is an infection caused by fungi, which are primitive organisms like mushrooms, mold and mildew that live in air, soil, plants and water, and some live in the human body. It often starts in the lungs or on the skin after spores are inhaled or land on you, and you are more likely to get one if your immune system is weakened or you take antibiotics.
about.next_step: See a doctor promptly if the skin or nail area is spreading, painful, not improving with basic care, or if you have fever, breathing symptoms, or a weakened immune system.
about.why: Only about half of fungi are harmful and skin and nail infections can be treated with medicines applied directly or by mouth for serious infections, but a clinician needs to confirm the type and choose the right treatment.

care.reply: Gallstones are hard deposits in the gallbladder that can block bile flow and cause attacks, often after eating, with pain in the abdomen, back or under the right arm, and nausea or vomiting. If there are no symptoms right now, routine follow-up with a doctor is usually enough; if an attack is happening, rest and avoid fatty meals until you can be assessed.
care.next_step: Book a doctor visit within the next few days for evaluation and advice, and seek care the same day if pain starts.
care.why: Gallstones are common and often found incidentally; treatment is usually considered only with symptoms, and the most common treatment is gallbladder removal. What is uncertain is whether this person is having an active attack or is asymptomatic, which changes urgency.
